The spine is a separation the donor made but never stated as the point: a RUN is a property of the win rate alone -- the payoff never enters the calculation -- while a DRAWDOWN needs both p and b, because how far you fall depends on what the winners scattered through the fall give back. The expected WAITING TIME for a run, (1 - q^k) / (p * q^k), which turns 'will it happen' into 'how often': at a 45% win rate the first run of eight arrives every 263 trades, about fifteen months at four a week, so a decade of that system should contain about eight of them. And the percentage columns are computed by compounding rather than by multiplication: a 16R drawdown at 1% risk a trade is a fall of 14.8%, not 16%, and at 3% it is 38.1%, not 48%. WHY IT COSTS TO SHOW: a resting quote is a free option written to whoever takes it (Copeland and Galai 1983), and the quantity displayed is the size of that option. Hiding buys invisibility and pays in queue position, because display priority fills the shown part of every order before the hidden part of any of them; Bessembinder, Panayides and Venkataraman measured both halves on a market where the choice is explicit. WORKED EXAMPLE, TWO TABLES, ARITHMETIC VERIFIED IN PYTHON. A hundred tests of one level, display 200 every time. 58 traded under half, 22 traded over half without clearing, 6 cleared and price moved on, 14 cleared and refilled. The record bounds the true rate at 14% to 94% (the 80 blind tests could all have had it and none could have shown it) and estimates 70% only under an independence assumption the same data cannot check. SOURCE: old lesson 42 (Opening and Closing Auctions) was 4,468 words of MOC/MOO imbalance trading advice: a seven-band imbalance table whose expected-move column had already been stripped by an earlier pass, three 'strategies' (index-rebalance front-running, spoof detection, technical confluence), a position-size ladder keyed to imbalance size, four Signal Pilot integration blurbs, and a composite trader -- Tom Rivera, $180K account, 23 close trades, 2 winners, -$87,000, with three dated ES disasters. All of it is gone, Tom included. TWO donor ideas survive, both rebuilt from mechanism: (1) that the open and the close are batch auctions rather than continuous trading, and (2) that a market-on-open order is not the same instrument as a market order -- which the donor asserted ('it eliminates walking the book') and this rebuild disproves with arithmetic. METHOD, AND IT DISCHARGES SLOT 41'S PROMISE: slot 41 promised how a single clearing price is computed from a book of competing orders, why it can sit outside everything that traded around it, and what an order placed into one is agreeing to. FINDINGS, all from one hand-run book of thirteen limit orders (six buy, seven sell) plus a 2,600-share market buy and a 300-share market sell, against a session that traded 100.00-100.30 with a last print of 100.20: (1) THE CROSS PRINTS OUTSIDE THE SESSION. Executable volume peaks at 100.50 with 2,900 shares and no other price comes within 200, so the volume-maximising step decides it alone and the tie-breaks never run. 100.50 is two ticks above the session high, and the high is not a term in the calculation -- at 100.40 demand of 3,300 still exceeded supply of 2,700, and the rule's only instruction is to trade more shares. A market order in an auction is demand at every price the algorithm tests. (2) THE LEFTOVER SITS ON THE MARGINAL ORDER: 600 of the 800-lot at 100.50 go unfilled while everyone who offered below is filled in full. (3) ONE MORE SELLER IS WORTH 520. Adding 1,200 offered at 100.30 lifts supply there from 2,100 to 3,300, beating 2,900, so the cross moves to 100.30 and the buyer's bill falls from 261,300 to 260,780. (4) THE UNCOMFORTABLE THEOREM: walking a continuous ladder made of the identical sell limits fills the same 2,600 shares at an average of 100.2654 (200@100.0, 400@100.1, 500@100.2, 700@100.3, 600@100.4, 200@100.5) for 260,690 -- 610 less. The auction reached the SAME top price as the walk and charged it on every share instead of the tail. This is general: the clearing price clears the last matched share, so it can never be below the highest price the walk would reach, and it is levied on the whole quantity. A call auction is systematically better for the resting side and worse for the aggressive side; the difference is a transfer. (5) HE SET HIS OWN PRICE: his 2,600 shares were 90% of the matched volume (79% with the extra seller). If you are most of the cross, the clearing price is your own arithmetic, computed in public, and then paid. (6) WHAT AN MOO/MOC AGREES TO, stated: not to trade at the open but to be counted as demand at every price the rule tests; the LOO/LOC is the instrument that keeps a bound, trading fill risk for price risk. BOUNDS handle the donor's remaining content honestly: the walk comparison assumes a fixed book (a continuous book at the open is thinner precisely because the auction concentrates orders -- slot 41's third mechanism); venue tie-breaks differ and many venues impose a collar that would have stopped the 100.50 print; and the published imbalance is a public announcement, not a signal addressed to you -- a strong reason not to be positioned against the cross long before it is a reason to be positioned with it. PROMISES SLOT 43: the events with a known time and no published book -- earnings, rate decisions, monthly data -- and how to price holding through one.

FINDINGS: (1) THE CORRECTION THE DONOR NEEDED. The implied move is the break-even of the STRADDLE, but almost nobody buys the straddle; a single option breaks even at its own premium, roughly half. On the worked quote (stock 100, call 3.10, put 2.90, straddle 6.00, implied move 6.00%) the straddle needs 6.00% and the call needs 3.10% -- so the folk warning 'you must beat the implied move' overstates a call buyer's hurdle by about 1.94x and talks him out of fairly priced trades. The donor's own quiz had made exactly this error. (2) THE PAYOFF TABLE, exact at expiry on intrinsic value only, by realised move: at +4% the call earns +0.90 on 3.10 risked; at -4% it loses all 3.10 while the PUT holder, right about direction on that same day, collects only +1.10 on a 2.90 premium and is still behind. Four per cent is a huge day, both traders called a direction correctly, one lost everything and the other lost most of it -- and nothing went wrong: the band was quoted at six and the move came in at four. (3) THE SHORT STRADDLE COLUMN collects on every row inside the band and pays outside it: a payoff shape, not an edge, distinguishable only over enough events to see the tail (lesson 19's arithmetic). (4) 'TRADE THE REACTION' AS ARITHMETIC, which is the new load-bearing content: a 1% stop against a publicly quoted 6% move is a stop the market has already priced through -- the quote says expected travel is six times the stop distance and about half of it runs in the direction that takes you out. Lesson 40 then charges for it: a 2% risk budget carried through an announcement is 3% at the module's median overshoot, 4% at the mean and 9% at the worst; sizing so the worst lands on 2% means trading at 0.44%. (5) STANDING ASIDE PRICED, on 252 sessions, sitting out the session before and after each event: 4 events -> 8 sessions -> 3.2% -> 1.03x; 12 -> 24 -> 9.5% -> 1.11x; 24 -> 48 -> 19.0% -> 1.24x; 48 -> 96 -> 38.1% -> 1.62x. At that sd a fairly priced straddle loses its buyer money 57.5 per cent of the time, which disposes of 'premium sellers win most of their trades' as evidence of anything. That asymmetry is why sizing by volatility is free and cutting for edge decay is not. THREE donor ideas survive. (1) That the stock/bond correlation has no fixed sign -- kept and turned into exact algebra. (2) That correlation rises in a crisis -- kept, mechanised, and then partly retracted. (3) The sensitivity division the source used to show a hedge had become a second copy of the position -- kept as the beta identity. NEW, computed in /tmp/build/corr.py on the module's sixty closes plus a second series built from them by a published rule (each return = 0.5 x the first series' return plus 0.866 of its return 29 bars later, wrapping): (a) The beta identity, verified: covariance over variance gives 0.4374, and correlation 0.4518 times the volatility ratio 0.9682 gives 0.4374. Correlation and sensitivity are one fact, so a hedge can carry the right sign and the wrong size. (b) A hedge removes rho squared of the variance, not rho: 0.3 removes 9 per cent and leaves 95 per cent of the standard deviation; 0.7 removes 49 and leaves 71; only 0.95 leaves under a third. (c) The window a third time. Rolling correlations on this pair span -0.41 to 0.94 at ten bars, a range of 1.35 on a scale that spans 2, narrowing to 0.92 at twenty and 0.78 at thirty. Fisher intervals price the noise: an observed 0.50 sits inside 0.07 to 0.77 on 20 observations, 0.28 to 0.67 on 60, and 0.40 to 0.59 on a full year of 252. (d) The sign is the relative size of two shocks, exactly. Writing shares as growth minus rates and bonds as minus growth minus rates, the correlation is (var rates - var growth) / (var rates + var growth): -0.50 at three-to-one growth, +0.50 at three-to-one rates, -0.80 and +0.80 at nine to one, and exactly zero when they balance -- where a measured zero means two strong opposite relationships rather than none. (e) Why it rises, in three mechanisms and no fear: a common factor whose variance grows takes rho from 0.25 to 0.75 with no loading and no behaviour changed; a leveraged holder's liquidation is a new factor lasting as long as the selling; and the measurement is biased upward by conditioning on a volatile stretch, with Forbes and Rigobon's adjustment turning an observed 0.80 into an unconditional 0.55 when variance quadruples, 0.60 into 0.35 and 0.90 into 0.72. Longin and Solnik are cited against it, and the disagreement is stated as the honest state of the question. (f) THE WORKED RESULT: the effective number of independent bets, N / (1 + (N-1) rho), which depends on the average pairwise correlation and nothing else about the structure. Twenty names at 0.3 carry 2.99 independent bets; at 0.1 they carry 6.90; at 0.8 they carry 1.23. Book risk rises 55.5 per cent from 0.3 to 0.8 with nobody trading, and holding it flat needs 35.7 per cent off every position -- a cut lesson 44's per-position volatility sizing cannot see. Diversification has an exact floor at the square root of the average correlation: 0.55 at rho 0.3, 0.89 at 0.8. DISCLOSED twice: the second series is constructed, and the rotation leaks -0.07 into the original, which is why the realised correlation is 0.45 rather than the 0.50 the weights aim at. Sources: Galton 1888, Fisher 1915, Markowitz 1952, Longin and Solnik 2001, Forbes and Rigobon 2002.

Three classes: blind to every reordering (mean, sd, high, low, median), blind to reversal alone (efficiency ratio 0.618 unchanged reversed but 1.000 sorted; lag-1 autocorrelation -0.0773 unchanged reversed, 0.1437 sorted), and order-seeing (net change, regression slope, RSI). (c) LAG IS THE FIRST MOMENT: SMA(10) and EMA(alpha=2/11) both have mean lag exactly 4.5000 and both pass exactly 0.10000 of the input variance, closed forms (n-1)/2, (1-a)/a and a/(2-a); WMA(10) is genuinely faster at 3.0000 = (n-1)/3 and pays 0.12727 = 385/3025, 27 per cent more noise. So the standard SMA-versus-EMA speed claim is false in both senses that can be made precise. (d) THE FRONTIER, the worked example: minimising sum of squared weights subject to unit sum and fixed mean lag gives weights linear in lag, so the efficient filters are the straight-line ones. Minimum sum of squares runs 0.10000 at lag 4.5, 0.10303 at 4.0, 0.11212 at 3.5, 0.12727 at 3.0 and 0.14848 at 2.5 -- the first half-bar of speed costs 3 per cent more noise, the third costs 13, and the exchange rate worsens all the way down. The plain SMA and the WMA both sit ON the frontier, not near it. The oldest weight reaches zero at lag 2.6667; below that every efficient filter must use negative weights, which is exactly what a low-lag or zero-lag smoother is doing and exactly why it overshoots. THE RESULT THE PAGE TURNS ON, which the source did not have: the displacement is not noise and not a tendency, it is FORCED. A pivot-low rule marks bar t precisely because closes t+1..t+k are all above it, so C[t+k] > C[t] is a logical consequence of the signal existing. Verified true for every pivot at k=2,3,5. The magnitude is the empirical part and the table separates it from an unselected bar over the same span: k=2 nine signals, mean +1.00, smallest +0.50, unconditional +0.18 (5.4x); k=3 four signals, +0.80, +0.20, +0.21 (3.9x); k=5 three signals, +1.87, +0.70, +0.31 (6.0x). Every minimum positive, not merely every mean. WORKED EXAMPLE: one rule, two columns. Long the two-bar pivot low, exit the next two-bar pivot high, seven round trips. As drawn: +20.40 pts, mean +2.91, seven winners and NO losing trade, profit factor undefined, and adverse excursion in the first two bars of exactly 0.00 on all seven, because a pivot low is the lowest close in its neighbourhood. As knowable (entries and exits two bars later): +3.90, mean +0.56, four winners, profit factor 2.39, adverse excursion mean 0.33 and worst 1.40. The gap is 16.50 points = 80.9 per cent, and it RECONCILES EXACTLY: entry displacement +1.0286 mean (all positive, forced) plus exit displacement -1.3286 (all negative, forced) is 2.3571 per trade, times seven, is 16.50 to the last decimal. So the tell people quote is the win rate and the real tell is the drawdown: a curve with no adverse excursion at all has usually chosen its entries from the far side of the outcome.
